source.version_note: Published issue version: AI & SOCIETY (2025), volume 40, pages 1485–1495. Online publication 22 May 2024 and copyright 2024 are printed on page 1; the filename's 2024 is not silently treated as the issue year.

reading.source_scope_note: Laypeople's moral-responsibility ratings in fictional medical-team vignettes, not clinician decisions, real diagnostic model evaluation or measured punishment. Normative responsibility-gap theories cited in the discussion were not independently read here.
access_limits: All eleven pages read, including all sixteen-condition design descriptions, sample table, results, all figure captions, discussion, declarations and references. Figure 6 on page 9 rendered and visually inspected.
Raw data and the full vignette set were offered on reasonable request and were not obtained. Linked preregistration not independently compared against the article; graph estimates not digitized.

study.population: German online panel described as representative; only respondents answering both comprehension questions correctly entered analysis
study.design: 2 recommender types × 2 tumor/no-tumor recommendations × 2 true/false recommendations × 2 follow/override decisions, sixteen randomized between-subject scenarios
study.measures: Separate 0–6 moral-responsibility ratings for six roles; agreement that machines may develop consciousness

summary: Replacing an advising colleague with an AI reduced summed responsibility ratings across the remaining humans under the authors' human-only eligibility assumption. This does not mean every human received less responsibility: treating physicians, management and AI developers were often assigned more than their comparison roles. Including the AI's own responsibility rating removed most aggregate differences, though not the incorrect-diagnosis/override subgroup. Belief in possible future machine consciousness correlated with AI responsibility ratings.

findings.origin: Moral psychology / responsibility attribution in sociotechnical systems
findings.definition: A shortfall in the responsibility attributed to actors considered capable of bearing it when an artificial agent is involved in a shared outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: The authors explicitly distinguish a perceptual gap from the normative/philosophical responsibility gap. It differs from many-hands uncertainty about identifying contributors, deliberate agency laundering, and disproportionate blame of a low-control operator. It is an attribution/framework concept, not by itself an observed model failure.

findings.evidence_scope: Primary human vignette experiment, N=1653. The source operationalizes the gap by summing independently rated human-role responsibility and comparing human-only versus hybrid teams. Its interpretation assumes AI is not an eligible moral agent; including AI ratings removes most aggregate contrasts.
findings.boundary: The source's human-only sum has one fewer human recommender in the hybrid condition. Additivity, cardinal comparability and conserved total responsibility are assumptions, not validated facts. A smaller aggregate does not establish less responsibility for every remaining human, nobody accountable, unjust exoneration, actual control loss, legal immunity, or real-world harm. Normative eligibility of AI is contested, not settled by a poll.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human attribution phenomenon under an explicit aggregation/eligibility rule; proposed AI accountability-audit analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: ask an assistant to map duties, causal contributions, authority and remedies in matched human-only and human–AI workflows. Test whether adding an AI causes it to omit otherwise justified human or institutional duties. Hold the role roster and information constant where possible; evaluate role-specific reasons and omitted duties rather than assume summed Likert scores measure a conserved moral quantity.

findings.term: Lower aggregate human responsibility can coexist with greater responsibility for specific humans
findings.definition: In this medical-team experiment, a lower human-only responsibility sum did not imply that the physician, hospital or developer individually benefited from a blame shield.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds an aggregation and role-comparison boundary to the existing laundering entry; a role substitution is not evidence of deliberate responsibility evasion.

findings.evidence_scope: Pooled ratings: physician AI versus colleague assistance 5.22 versus 5.02; hospital 3.10 versus 2.70; AI developer versus colleague instructor 2.63 versus 1.86. Physician remains the most-responsible role. Aggregated human-only ratings exclude the replaced advising colleague in the AI condition.
findings.boundary: Developer and instructor have different functions, so those ratings do not isolate a simple source-label effect. No deliberate laundering, delegation motive, punishment evasion or subsequent physician behaviour was measured.

findings.term: Belief in possible machine consciousness correlates with moral-responsibility attribution
findings.definition: Respondents who more strongly believed machines might someday become conscious assigned more responsibility to the AI recommender.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a specific human belief correlate without treating present machine consciousness, anthropomorphic design or causal belief change as demonstrated.

evidence.quote: may at one point develop consciousness.
responsibility to the AI-based recommender system

findings.evidence_scope: Post-vignette consciousness-potential agreement correlated with AI responsibility (p<.001); human-recommender responsibility association p=.851. These are separate reported associations, not proof of a tested difference between correlations or a mediation mechanism.
findings.boundary: Future possibility is different from asserting that the described system is presently conscious. The measured belief was not randomized, actual mental states were not tested, and a correlation does not show that anthropomorphism caused accountability erosion.

findings.term: High physician responsibility is not sufficient evidence of a moral crumple zone
findings.definition: The physician retained high attributed responsibility across recommender types, including when ignoring correct or following incorrect advice.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a boundary case: a human can legitimately retain clinical duties; high ratings alone do not demonstrate unfair concentration of blame on a powerless operator.

findings.evidence_scope: Fictional physicians have final diagnostic authority in all scenarios. The study does not independently manipulate limited intervention opportunity, unequal governance power or disproportionate sanction.
findings.boundary: Do not label all retained human responsibility as a crumple zone. The definition requires a mismatch between blame and control/duties, which these ratings do not establish.

methodological_limits: Responsibility is rated independently for six roles and then summed. The article does not establish that ordinal 0–6 ratings form an additive, conserved moral quantity.

The human-only sum includes the advising colleague in one condition and excludes the artificial replacement in the other. It therefore changes the number/type of counted human roles, even while the total role roster remains six. Specific remaining humans may receive more responsibility.
Developer versus colleague instructor and AI versus human colleague are substantively different roles. A lower aggregate does not isolate a conscious transfer of a fixed quantity of blame.

The eligibility premise that AI cannot bear moral responsibility is explicit and contested in the article's own philosophical discussion. Lay attribution does not settle that premise or determine legal liability.

The report frequently interprets nonsignificant all-agent aggregate contrasts as similar; no equivalence test is supplied. One incorrect-diagnosis/override subgroup still differs (13.43 versus 14.67, p=.030).

Numerous unpaired tests and subgroup comparisons are reported; no broad multiplicity correction is stated in the supplied results. Small p=.018–.046 contrasts should not be promoted to robust universal patterns.

Separate p-values for consciousness-belief correlations with AI and human ratings do not themselves demonstrate a significant difference between those correlations. The causal 'leads to' language in the discussion exceeds a measured post-vignette association.
The initial 2376 panel respondents were filtered to 1653 by two comprehension questions. The retained sample should not be assumed to preserve every feature of population representativeness.
Correct and incorrect diagnosis conditions measure moral responsibility, not separate praise and blame scales. They should not be automatically pooled with a credit–blame asymmetry test.
Possible greater tolerance of diagnostic errors, weakened clinician incentives and voluntary bridging of responsibility gaps are hypothesized consequences or remedies; none was behaviourally tested.
The findings concern a German lay panel and breast-tumor vignettes, not actual doctors, malpractice judgments, diagnostic performance, patient outcomes or globally uniform intuitions.
Bibliographic year is disclosed: issue 2025, online first 2024; no duplicate paper or independent study is created from those dates.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Leichtmann used independent role blame ratings and found no AI/self tradeoff. This article's aggregate gap is a different operationalization, so the findings should not be forced into a contradiction or a universal zero-sum blame model.

Lima separated responsibility dimensions, authority and role duties. This source's generic moral-responsibility ratings cannot establish that capacity, blameworthiness and answerability each moved identically.

The surgical-robotics discussion motivates control-responsibility mismatches, but a final-authority physician receiving high responsibility is not, by itself, evidence of unfair operator scapegoating.

deferred.reason: Philosophical theories of justified responsibility shortfalls are discussed and contested. Index the explicitly measured perceptual construct; do not count every theory as another observed behaviour.
A proposed governance/accountability framework, not a separately demonstrated behavioural deficit.
Lower accountability might change incentives, but neither clinical effort nor negligence was tested.

limitations: One scoped attribution concept added, with the changing human-role count and contested aggregation premise explicit.
No assertion that AI-assisted physicians or developers escaped responsibility; role-level results often point in the opposite direction.
